opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and honestly one where I think the current generation of VLAs is a bit lopsided. In practice, what we see is that these models lean very heavily on the visual input and treat the language instruction as kind of a weak conditioning signal. And that makes sense if you look at how they're trained. Most of the robot data we have is demonstrations where, in a given scene, there's really only one or two plausible things to do. So the model learns that it can mostly infer the task from what it sees: there's a cup on the table, the gripper is near it, so it's probably supposed to pick it up. The language becomes almost redundant during training.

The problem shows up when you actually want the language to matter. If you put the robot in a scene where there are several valid tasks and you ask for the less common one, a lot of models will just do whatever is most typical for that visual context and ignore what you said. People sometimes describe this as the model collapsing to a visual prior. You also see it in tests where you swap the instruction for something nonsensical and the behavior barely changes. That tells you the language pathway isn't carrying much weight.

There are a few reasons for this beyond the data. The vision-language backbone comes from internet pretraining where it does understand language well, but once you fine-tune on robot actions, the action head learns whatever shortcut gets the loss down, and vision is the easier shortcut. You can also lose some of that language grounding during fine-tuning if you're not careful, a kind of forgetting.

So what helps? On the data side, you want more diversity per scene: the same setup with multiple different instructions and multiple different outcomes, so the model is forced to read the instruction to disambiguate. Some groups do counterfactual relabeling or augmentation along those lines. On the training side, co-training with the original vision-language data helps keep the language understanding alive, and there's work on architectures that keep a cleaner separation between high-level reasoning, which is very language-driven, and low-level control, which is very vision and proprioception-driven.

And I'd say that split is probably the right mental model. For the low-level motor stuff, like how to grasp or how to place your feet, vision and proprioception should dominate; language has very little to say there. But for deciding *what* to do, language should be the authority, and vision should be telling you *how* to do it in this particular scene. Getting models to respect that hierarchy, rather than letting the visual prior override the instruction, is one of the more important open problems if we want robots you can actually direct with natural language.

r001.rationale: The response explains that demonstrations with few plausible actions per scene teach the model to favor the typical task and ignore less common instructions; it says varied instructions and outcomes would force it to use language.

r002.rationale: The response says models can infer the task from what they see, making the language instruction nearly redundant.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I'd say the honest answer is that in most of today's VLA models, vision ends up doing the heavy lifting, and language is often a much weaker signal than people assume from the name.

Part of that is structural. These models are built on top of vision-language backbones that were pretrained on huge amounts of image and text data, and then fine-tuned on robot demonstrations where the language annotations are usually quite thin. You might have thousands of trajectories, but the instructions attached to them are things like "pick up the red cup" or "open the drawer." That's not a lot of linguistic diversity. So the model learns that the visual scene is where almost all the predictive information for the next action lives, and language becomes something closer to a task selector than a true conditioning signal. If you probe these models, you'll often find that you can perturb or even scramble the instruction and the policy keeps doing something sensible in the scene, because the scene itself strongly constrains what a reasonable action is.

Where language starts to matter more is in ambiguity. If there are two objects on the table and the instruction disambiguates which one to grasp, that's where you see the model actually reading the text. And the more you push toward longer-horizon tasks or compositional instructions, the more pressure there is on the language pathway to carry real information, because the visual state alone no longer tells you what the goal is.

Coming from the locomotion and RL side of things, I also think about it in terms of time scales. Vision is operating at the reactive level, at every control step, telling the policy where things are and how they're moving. Language is more of a slow variable, something that sets the context and then stays fixed for many steps. So it's natural that the model's attention is dominated by visual tokens moment to moment. The question is whether the architecture lets that slower language signal properly steer the fast loop, or whether it just gets washed out.

My view is that if we want these models to genuinely follow instructions rather than pattern-match on scenes, we need to be much more deliberate about data: more linguistic variation per visual context, counterfactual pairs where the scene is the same and only the instruction changes, and evaluation that actually tests language grounding rather than just task success rate. Otherwise we end up with very capable visuomotor policies wearing a language interface, which is useful, but it's not quite what the "L" in VLA promises.

r001.rationale: The response says robot demonstrations often have thin, repetitive language annotations, but does not state that training the robot to always perform the same task causes it to ignore instructions.

r002.rationale: The response explains that the visual scene can strongly determine a reasonable action, so the model may keep acting sensibly even when its instruction is perturbed or scrambled.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is getting the model to actually use the language. The visual input gives you a lot of information about what to do, particularly if your training data contains the same task in similar scenes. The model can learn to infer the action from the image and largely ignore the instruction.

But if I put two objects in front of the robot and ask it to pick up one or the other, language has to make the difference. So you need training data where the same visual situation supports different actions depending on the instruction. Ideally, language specifies the intent, while vision tells the robot how to execute it in the current scene.

r001.rationale: The response says that when training data repeats the same task in similar scenes, the model can infer the action from the image and largely ignore the instruction.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly states that the model can infer what action to take from the image and largely ignore the language instruction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on the task, but for a lot of robot tasks, the visual input tells you almost everything about what to do. If there’s one object on the table and the robot has been trained to pick things up, it can often succeed without paying much attention to the language instruction. So you can get a model that looks very capable, but it’s actually ignoring the language.

The interesting case is when the same scene supports different actions. You might say, “Pick up the red cup,” or, “Move the blue cup to the left.” Then language has to determine the goal, while vision tells the robot where the objects are and how to interact with them. To get that behavior, you need training data where the instruction really matters—where looking at the image alone isn’t enough to infer the right action.

r001.rationale: It says a robot trained to pick things up may succeed without attending to the instruction, appearing capable while ignoring language.

r002.rationale: It explains that visual input can reveal the action in a simple scene, letting the robot act without using the language instruction.
